newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: Shots fired at Central African Republic minister.
newsitem.headline: Shots fired at Central African Republic minister.

text.p: Shots have been fired at Central African Republic's defence minister in the capital Bangui, where tension between President Ange-Felix Patasse's supporters and army mutineers persists, witnesses and officials said.

Presidential spokesman Prosper Ndouba told state television that Defence Minister Pascal Kado had escaped unhurt on Saturday after his car was fired on in Bangui's Petevo district, a rebel stronghold.
A rebel spokesman described the presence of Kado, who is close to fellow northerner Patasse, as a provocative, saying he should have informed the mutineers' of his plan to go there.

African mediators, led by Mali's widely respected former military leader General Amadou Toumani Toure, are trying to broker peace in the impoverished nation after three army revolts in less than a year.

The revolts -- last April, May and latterly from November -- began over pay but broadened into an attempt to topple Patasse, a northern civilian elected in 1993. French troops helped calm the latest revolt before handing over to African peacekeepers.
Bangui was calm on Sunday but residents report a spate of shooting incidents and armed robberies.
Patasse's spokesman, speaking late on Saturday, condemned the incident involving the defence minister without directly blaming the mutineers.

African peacekeepers clashed with mutineers and their supporters March 22 and 23. At least five people were killed. The clashes were the worst since Patasse and his rivals agreed a peace plan on January 25.
Patasse has twice met the mutineers' leaders in April but tensions persist.
The mutineers' leader, Captain Anicet Saulet, told French radio on Saturday that they were demanding guarantees to cover their return to barracks.
The mutineers are from the minority southern Yakoma tribe of former military leader Andre Kolingba, their rivals are northern Patasse loyalists in the presidential guard.

Saulet said that Patasse had made a step forward on the political level by nominating two officers chosen by the mutineers to a government of national unity but he had to make concessions on the military front.

"We want the post of deputy armed forces chief of staff," he said, adding that the mutineers -- referred to locally as ex-mutineers -- wanted joint command of the different units within the armed forces to ease their return.
Around 500 soldiers from Mali, Senegal, Gabon, Chad, Burkina Faso and Togo serve with the African peacekeeping force.
